ersteHilfe.title: How to start your mediation
ersteHilfe.text: No complicated procedure – a clear, guided path from the first click to an agreement.

steps.title: Open your case online
steps.text: Describe your conflict in a few minutes – anonymously and without obligation. No lawyer, no in-person appointment.

steps.title: Invite the other side and work out interests
steps.text: The other side is invited in a neutral way. Together you set a date for the first conversation.

steps.title: Find a joint solution
steps.text: In a structured and fair way, you work out a solution both sides can live with – put down in writing.

faq.q: Does the other side have to agree right away?
faq.a: No. You first open your case on your own. Only afterwards is the other side invited – neutrally and without accusations.

faq.q: What does the first step cost?
faq.a: Nothing. Your account and opening your case are free and non-binding – the actual mediation starts with the entry plan from €49 per party.
The final agreement is a binding contract. For legally complex matters, it should also be reviewed by a lawyer or notary.

zweiWelten.title: Two worlds. One principle.
zweiWelten.intro: At the kitchen table or in the boardroom: conflicts follow the same patterns – and can be resolved with the same method.

privat.title: Conflicts that live at home.
privat.text: Separation, inheritance, neighbours: the dispute sits at the table every evening and wears down the relationship that still has to work afterwards. We give it a framework in which both sides are heard – at a fixed price, not by the hour.

business.title: Conflicts that cost money every day.
business.text: Shareholder disputes, team conflicts, B2B: the dispute blocks decisions, ties up management time and damages the business relationship that still has to work afterwards. Court proceedings take years – our process takes six steps.

tabs.label: Separation
tabs.title: Divorce mediation online.
tabs.intro: Separation and divorce don't just mean emotional strain – they also mean concrete decisions: support, childcare, finances. That is exactly what divorce mediation is for – a structured process that leads both sides to a workable arrangement, even when their ideas are far apart.

features.title: Different expectations
features.text: Both sides have clear expectations – but no common ground on what a fair solution could look like.

features.title: Emotions block conversations
features.text: Hurt and disappointment make it hard to talk calmly about support or childcare.

features.title: Pressure from time and money
features.text: Financial uncertainty and the need for quick decisions add further pressure to the conflict.

tabs.label: Neighbours
tabs.title: When everyday life becomes a conflict.
tabs.intro: Neighbourhood mediation is a guided process in which neighbours work out binding arrangements with a mediator. Neighbour disputes often start small: noise, boundaries, parking, gardens or house rules. They become difficult because you can't simply avoid each other.

features.title: Recurring annoyance
features.text: Noise, rubbish, parking or boundaries keep coming up and weigh on everyday life.

features.title: Communication has broken down
features.text: Conversations are avoided, turn aggressive or only happen through complaints.

features.title: Permanent proximity
features.text: The conflict doesn't go away on its own, because the people involved run into each other regularly.

tabs.label: Inheritance
tabs.title: When an estate becomes a test of endurance.
tabs.intro: Inheritances are rarely just a question of money. Grief, expectations, old roles and different ideas of fairness often collide.

features.title: Different expectations
features.text: Some want to sell, others want to keep. Some feel disadvantaged, others feel passed over.

features.title: Old family patterns
features.text: Conflicts from the past resurface and block objective decisions.

features.title: Property or businesses
features.text: It gets particularly difficult when assets can't simply be divided or come with responsibility.

tabs.label: Business & ODR
tabs.title: When conflicts paralyse the company.
tabs.intro: Online dispute resolution (ODR) means conflicts are settled entirely digitally – structured, strictly confidential and much faster than court proceedings. Whether it's a dispute between business partners, within the company, in e-commerce or a conciliation with a concrete proposal: medipact maps the right type of procedure online. The most expensive item in a business conflict is rarely the invoice – it's management's tied-up attention: weeks in which decisions should be made instead of arguments.

features.title: Team & department mediation
features.text: The classic: friction in project teams, entrenched fronts between departments (e.g. IT vs. business units) or conflicts after restructuring.

features.title: Leadership mediation
features.text: Conflicts at management level, between levels of hierarchy – and the classic tension between management and the works council.

features.title: Shareholders & succession
features.text: Disputes within the founding team or among shareholders over direction, shares or exit – and the emotional handover to the next generation in a family business.

tabs.label: Consumers
tabs.title: When the invoice and the work don't match.
tabs.intro: Disputed invoices, defects or services not delivered: with small amounts at stake, going to court rarely pays off – but the annoyance remains unresolved.

features.title: Disputed invoice
features.text: The final price is well above the estimate – and nobody wants to give in.

features.title: Defects & remedial work
features.text: The work has defects, but deadlines, warranty and responsibility are disputed.

features.title: Blocked communication
features.text: Complaints go unanswered – or are only met with pressure through payment reminders.

tabs.label: Tenancy
tabs.title: The dispute ends, the tenancy continues.
tabs.intro: Service charges, defects, deposits, owner's own use: tenancy disputes are rarely a purely legal matter. Usually it's about a statement nobody explained, defects left unaddressed for too long – and two sides who still have to deal with each other afterwards.

features.title: The statement doesn't explain itself
features.text: A four-figure back payment arrives without explanation. A large part of the dispute resolves itself simply through access to receipts and a comprehensible calculation.

features.title: Withholding payment escalates things
features.text: Anyone who reduces or withholds rent often has good reasons – but at the same time risks termination for late payment. A defect thus turns into a dispute about whether the tenancy continues at all.

features.title: Deadlines run in the background
features.text: Billing deadline, objection deadline, objection to termination, eviction deadline: in tenancy law it's often not the better argument that wins, but whoever responded in time.

tabs.label: Workplace
tabs.title: Before the conflict turns into a resignation.
tabs.intro: Workplace conflicts are rarely fought out in the open. They show up as sick days, as emails with four people in CC, as a team taking sides – and eventually as a resignation. Until then, nobody has talked to the other side.

features.title: Communication moves to writing
features.text: Conversations are replaced by emails, people are copied in, agreements are confirmed "just to be safe". That's not a need for order, it's gathering evidence – and therefore a step towards escalation.

features.title: Absences pile up
features.text: An unresolved conflict measurably makes people ill. When someone's sick days correlate with a particular constellation, the conflict is already a cost factor.

features.title: The team takes sides
features.text: What starts as a dispute between two people ties up half the department within a few weeks. By then, the original parties are far from the only ones affected.

home.processTitle: 6 clear steps towards a possible agreement.
home.processText: Guided rather than left on your own, based on the Harvard principle – fair to all sides.

processSteps.title: Describe the conflict
processSteps.text: You describe the situation from your point of view – confidentially and at your own pace. The other side is invited fairly.

processSteps.title: Guided process
processSteps.text: Six structured phases based on the Harvard principle: from collecting topics through interests to fair options.

processSteps.title: Binding agreement
processSteps.text: At the end there is a concrete agreement: who does what by when – recorded and confirmed by both sides.

home.processLinkEinigung: Why this works at a fixed price
home.processLinkPersoenlich: Prefer a mediator? Start digitally, continue in person

starter.title: Sort things out together first.
starter.titleHighlight: Then continue with the mediator you choose.
starter.text: You and the other side work out digitally what the conflict is about and what really matters to you – each at your own pace, no appointment needed. Then you meet mediators and hand over to the one who suits you. They don't start from scratch.

phasen.title: Introduction
phasen.text: Clarify your concern, the process and confidentiality. You invite the other side – they are involved from the start.

phasen.title: Collect the issues
phasen.text: Both sides note separately what needs to be resolved. Clear questions guide you, each at your own pace.

phasen.title: Work out interests
phasen.text: What lies behind the positions? Needs, worries and what really counts – set side by side for both parties.

phasen.title: Handover to your mediator
phasen.text: Up to 3 introductory calls of 20 minutes each. The person you choose takes over with everything you have prepared.

mission.statement: Most conflicts don't need a court.
mission.text: They need a process that holds. Because a dispute doesn't just cost money: it costs months in which nothing is decided, and it costs the relationship that still has to work afterwards. Anyone who adds that up beforehand decides differently. medipact gives the dispute a structure – clear steps, equal rights for both sides, trained mediators – so that in the end, you decide, not the escalation.

didYouKnowFacts.text: The Harvard Negotiation Project was founded in 1979. It produced the 1981 worldwide bestseller "Getting to Yes" by Roger Fisher and William Ury – the basis of the principle medipact implements digitally today: interests, not positions.

Since 26 July 2012, the German Mediation Act has governed mediation as an independent, legally recognised procedure – based on an EU directive intended to strengthen out-of-court dispute resolution throughout Europe.
Section 4 of the German Mediation Act legally obliges the mediator to keep confidential everything discussed during the mediation – with only a few, clearly defined exceptions.

Section 1 of the German Mediation Act defines the mediator as an independent, neutral person without any decision-making authority. Unlike a court judgment, only the parties themselves determine the outcome.

didYouKnowFacts.eyebrow: An agreement becomes a binding document
didYouKnowFacts.text: A mediation agreement is initially a private-law contract – but it can be made legally binding and enforceable, for example through notarisation or a settlement concluded by lawyers.

Since the Mediation Act reformed Section 278 (5) of the German Code of Civil Procedure, courts can refer parties to a specially trained "conciliation judge" – a further sign that an out-of-court agreement is often the better first route.

didYouKnowFacts.eyebrow: Costs must be clear up front
didYouKnowFacts.text: Section 2 (4) of the German Mediation Act requires the mediator to inform the parties of the expected costs of the procedure at the outset – so transparency is not a courtesy but a legal duty.

didYouKnowFacts.eyebrow: Four principles instead of negotiating tactics
didYouKnowFacts.text: The Harvard concept rests on four principles: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain and insist on objective criteria. medipact structures digital mediation along exactly these four steps.

"Getting to Yes" coined the term BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) – the best alternative if no agreement is reached. Knowing your BATNA lets you negotiate with more confidence and keeps you from being pushed into a worse outcome.

Since 1981, "Getting to Yes" has been translated into more than 35 languages and sold over 15 million copies. Principled negotiation still shapes business, diplomacy and – via the Mediation Act – German law today.

quickCheck.title: Is mediation right for your situation?

questions.text: If the other side called you today to talk about a solution – would you pick up?
Can you imagine that the other side would describe the situation very differently – and still have an understandable point?
Imagine the conflict were resolved in four weeks. Would your everyday life feel noticeably easier?
Can you tell the other side what you really think without it being used against you later?
Have you already invested your own time, energy or money that you don't want to simply write off?
Are there currently threats, massive pressure or fear that make an open conversation impossible?
questions.hint: If so: mediation is no substitute for protection – please talk to a counselling service or a lawyer first.
